pages.text:
*Ama's Stall Ledger, Night 14. Bowls sold: 52. A handful: 31 grams (approximately). Ama says: stop weighing my hands.*

I stole a digital kitchen scale from Ma’s cabinet and a set of plastic measuring spoons from the drawer. I hid them under the counter, right next to the soy sauce, because secrets feel safer when they are close to salt.

My plan was simple. Ama sat in her boss chair, the one with the wobbly leg she refused to fix. Every time she called out "a handful," I would catch it in a tin bowl and weigh it. I thought if I could just find the number, the mystery would stop.

Ama watched me weigh the star anise. She leaned forward, her elbows on her knees, watching the little screen change numbers. She looked at me the way a cat watches a mouse trying to explain the concept of being eaten.

"Lin," she said softly. "Are you counting my teeth?"

"No," I said, my voice very small. "I am checking the math."

"Math does not cook," she said, turning back to the pot.
pages.image: A small girl with a black bob and green jacket crouches under a stall counter holding a digital scale and tin bowl, while a sturdy grandmother with silver curls watches from a wobbly plastic chair with amused, sharp eyes.

pages.text:
The numbers refused to behave. On Tuesday, a handful of star anise weighed thirty-one grams. On Wednesday, it dropped to twenty-two. By Thursday, it had jumped to thirty-eight. I was losing my mind, and I was definitely losing my faith in the universe.

I slammed the tin bowl onto the counter. The clatter made Uncle Feng look up from his oysters. "Which one is right?" I demanded, pointing at the digital scale. "There has to be a right number."

Ama did not look up from her ladle. She was stirring the broth with that slow, circular motion that never hurried. "The one the weather wants," she said.

"The weather is not an ingredient."

"It is," she replied, finally turning to face me. "When it is colder, the beef needs more ginger to wake it up. When the air is heavy with humidity, too much sugar makes the broth feel like mud. You do not add the same thing every day. That is why it tastes alive."

I looked down at my neat little notebook. My lines were straight. My numbers were tidy. And yet, the pot was doing something messy and wonderful that my list could not catch. It was like trying to measure the length of a joke with a ruler. The water kept moving.
pages.image: A close up of a steaming soup pot where a grandmother’s hand holds a wooden ladle, while a girl with a pencil behind her ear looks frustrated at a small digital scale and tin bowl on the counter.

pages.text:
I stopped trying to force the numbers to match and started listening to the pot instead. The water changed pitch when the beef got tender, and I noticed that the rain tapping on the tarp meant the customers would be tired and want something warm. Even the beef itself seemed to have an opinion. Sometimes it arrived tough from the butcher and needed an extra hour of patience, while other times it yielded quickly, like a shy classmate finally answering a question.

It was not a list. It was a conversation.

I opened my spiral notebook and crossed out the column for "exact grams." The pencil tip snapped under the pressure, leaving a small graphite shard on the paper. I did not care. I wrote a new heading in big, careful letters.

RECIPE = LISTENING.

I underlined it once, then realized that one underline was not enough for a truth this important, so I underlined it again. The pencil broke completely this time. I did not care. For the first time, I felt like I was actually learning how to cook, not just how to measure. I was learning how to listen.
pages.image: Lin, an eleven-year-old girl with a chin-length black bob and straight bangs, in a dark green padded jacket and a red-and-white checked apron, writes in a spiral notebook with a pencil, focused and serious, while Ama in her flowery vest stirs a big steaming pot beside her at a night-market stall.

pages.text:
Ama clapped her hands together and nudged me toward the pot. "Now, the nose. Smell the foam. What does it want?"

I leaned in close. The aroma was rich and deep, with a sharp edge that felt like the last bite of a good snack. My brain was still trying to calculate minutes, but my nose already knew. It understood that the broth was too thick and needed a little more water to let the flavors breathe.

"It wants space," I said.

Ama nodded. "Good. Now, skim the top."

She showed me how to use the ladle to scoop away the grey foam floating on the surface. "Gently," she whispered. "If you rush it, the broth turns cloudy. Cloudy is sad. Clear is happy."

I practiced, but I scooped too hard once and pulled up a whole chunk of braised beef. Panic flared in my chest, but Ama just pointed at my mouth.

I ate the beef. It was the best piece of meat I had ever tasted, better than any school-cafeteria meatball I had ever eaten, and I did not even need to count the seconds.
pages.image: A girl in a red-and-white checked apron carefully skimming foam from a large pot with a brass ladle, her face close to the steam, while a grandmother points at her mouth with a smile.

pages.text:
By the end of the week, people in the lane started talking.

"Does it matter if I have the girl's bowl or Ama's bowl?" asked a man in a wool coat.

Ama shrugged. "Ask the girl."

I pretended to be busy wiping a table. I did not look at them. I did not smile. I certainly did not feel a warm glow of pride spreading through my chest, which was definitely not happening.

Ama watched me for a long moment. Then she reached for her red ledger. She wrote the bowl count. Then, in her own careful pencil, she added a small tick in a new column she had drawn herself.

I peeked over her shoulder. "What is that?"

"Good," Ama said, turning away to wipe a table that was already clean. "Now go count the stools. They keep wandering."
pages.image: A grandmother with short silver hair writing a small tick in a red notebook, while a girl in a green jacket and checked apron peeks over her shoulder with a surprised and pleased expression.
